To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
NOMA is more suitable for the cell center users than the cell-edge users in the downlink under a realistic traffic model.
NOMA with SUC in a realistic traffic model can provide significant system-level throughput gain compared to OMA in a cellular downlink.

the throughput gain of NOMA with successive interference cancellation (SIC) over orthogonal multiple access (OFDMA) is more significant under a realistic finite-payload file transfer protocol (FTPT) traffic model than under the full-buffer traffic assumption, and that the throughput gain is maximized by a user scheduling criterion that assigns the strongest users to the strongest resource blocks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the investigation of the system-level throughput performance of NOMA with various user scheduling schemes under a realistic finite-payload FTP traffic model.
the system-level performance of NOMA with the realistic traffic model and the various user scheduling criteria.
the investigation of the system-level throughput and user scheduling in a realistic traffic model.

NOMA with SUCI is a promising candidate for 5G and beyond.
the throughput gain of NOMA with the realistic FTP traffic model is more significant than that of the full-buffer traffic, especially at the cell-edge users.
NOMA is a very promising multiple access technology in the 5G era, which can improve the system throughput and user experience.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NOMA with SLC has the potential to improve the cell edge user experience in the realistic traffic environment, while the performance gain is less pronounced in the vicinity of base station.
the throughput gain of NOMA in the vicinity of a cell can be translated to a significant gain in the cell-edge user throughput.
the system-level throughput performance of NOMA with an SIC in the downlink is highly dependent on the user scheduling criterion.
